```{r options, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7.5,
                      fig.height = 4.4, fig.align = "center", dpi = 96)
old_options <- options(digits = 3, width = 90)
has_ggplot <- requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE)
```

Individuals belonging to the same team, pupils attending the same classroom,
or repeated observations from the same student may share characteristics
because they belong to a common higher-level unit. Consequently, their
ratings may exhibit similarities that cannot be explained solely by
individual-level differences. The additive model introduced by Houle, Morin
and Harvey (2026) accounts for this hierarchical structure by identifying
latent group classes that differ in the average level of their members'
ratings. Unlike models that identify individual-level profiles, the additive
model does not classify individuals into separate latent profiles. Instead,
each group is assigned to a latent group class, and all individuals within
that group share the same group-level classification while retaining
individual variation around their group's estimated level. The group classes
can therefore be interpreted as distinct types of groups, rather than
subgroups of individuals. This distinction follows the person-centred
perspective, in which latent classifications are interpreted according to the
level at which the underlying heterogeneity occurs (Scrucca et al., 2024;
Saqr et al., 2024).

The framework extends beyond differences in group means through several
additional model specifications. The dispersion family identifies group
classes that differ in the extent of variation among their members, while the
additive-dispersion family simultaneously accounts for differences in group
means and within-group variability. Two further cross-level families allow
individual-level profiles and group-level classes to be estimated jointly,
thereby capturing heterogeneity at both levels of the hierarchical structure.

These model families are currently experimental. Their implementation
supports model estimation, standard errors, descriptive tables, graphical
representations, class enumeration, and bootstrap likelihood-ratio testing.
However, handling missing data and incorporating covariates are not yet
supported.

## The additive model

Consider a dataset consisting of $J$ groups, where group $j$ contains $n_j$
individuals who provide ratings on $d$ indicators. The additive model assumes
that each group belongs to one of $H$ latent group classes. The group-level
classification is represented by $C_j$, while $B_{jr}$ denotes the
group-specific intercept for indicator $r$. The model can be expressed as
follows:

$$
C_j \sim \operatorname{Categorical}(\omega_1,\ldots,\omega_H)
$$

$$
B_{jr}\mid C_j=h \sim N(\mu_{hr},T_{hr})
$$

$$
Y_{ijr}\mid B_{jr}\sim N(B_{jr},W_r).
$$

The first component specifies the probability of belonging to each latent
group class, with $\omega_h$ representing the proportion of groups belonging to
class $h$. The second component describes the distribution of group-specific
intercepts within each class. In particular, $\mu_{hr}$ represents the average
level of indicator $r$ for group class $h$, while $T_{hr}$ captures
between-group variability within that class. The third component specifies
the distribution of individual ratings around their respective group
intercepts, with $W_r$ representing the within-group variance for indicator
$r$.

The defining characteristic of the additive model is that the within-group
variance is constrained to be equal across all latent group classes. Thus,
the classes can differ in their average indicator levels and, when specified,
in their between-group variability, but not in the residual variation among
individuals within groups. This shared within-group variance distinguishes
the additive specification from models that also allow within-group
dispersion to vary across classes.

An additional computational advantage is that the likelihood can be evaluated
directly using the group sizes, group means, and within-group sums of
squares. Consequently, estimation does not require numerical integration,
making the model computationally tractable even when the analysis involves
multiple indicators and latent group classes.

## Data

The ratings below are simulated so that the truth is known: 120 teams of 4 to
12 members rate the team's climate and the support they receive. Teams are
of two types, supportive and strained, which differ in their average ratings
and, for climate, in how much teams of the type vary.

```{r data}
library(latents)
set.seed(2026)
n_teams <- 120
team_type <- rep(c("supportive", "strained"), times = c(66, 54))
team_size <- rep(c(4, 6, 8, 12), length.out = n_teams)
team_climate <- rnorm(n_teams, ifelse(team_type == "supportive", 0.8, -0.8),
                      ifelse(team_type == "supportive", 0.35, 0.6))
team_support <- rnorm(n_teams, ifelse(team_type == "supportive", 0.6, -0.5), 0.45)
ratings <- data.frame(
  team = rep(seq_len(n_teams), team_size),
  type = rep(team_type, team_size),
  climate = rep(team_climate, team_size) + rnorm(sum(team_size), 0, 0.9),
  support = rep(team_support, team_size) + rnorm(sum(team_size), 0, 1))
str(ratings)
```

The model never sees `type`; it is kept to check the classification later.

## Fitting

The additive model is a `family` of `multilpa()`. It takes the ratings, the
group column and the number of group classes; there is no `n_profiles`,
because there are no individual profiles.

```{r fit}
fit <- multilpa(ratings, c("climate", "support"), "team",
                n_group_classes = 2, family = "additive", seed = 1)
fit
```

## The number of group classes

Models with one, two and three classes are compared by BIC, which for this family
is penalized by the number of groups (`nobs(fit)` is the number of teams).

```{r classes}
fit_one <- multilpa(ratings, c("climate", "support"), "team",
                    n_group_classes = 1, family = "additive", seed = 1)
fit_three <- multilpa(ratings, c("climate", "support"), "team",
                      n_group_classes = 3, family = "additive", seed = 1)
BIC(fit_one, fit, fit_three)
```

Two classes have the lowest BIC. The three-class fit also warns that a
between-group variance went to zero: with a third class there is no
between-team spread left for some class to explain. A likelihood-ratio test of
two against three classes needs a bootstrap reference distribution, not the
chi-square; `bootstrap_lrt()` provides it, as shown below for one against two
classes.

## Differences in spread between classes

`between_variance = "equal"` constrains the between-group variances to be
equal across classes, which leaves the classes differing in location only.

```{r restriction}
fit_equal <- multilpa(ratings, c("climate", "support"), "team",
                      n_group_classes = 2, family = "additive",
                      between_variance = "equal", seed = 1)
BIC(fit, fit_equal)
AIC(fit, fit_equal)
```

Both criteria prefer the equal-spread model, although the data were simulated
with more spread in climate among strained teams. With 120 teams that
difference is too small to be told apart from sampling noise, which is what
the criteria report. The rest of this article uses the varying model to show
every parameter.

## Comparing the group-class families

`enumerate_classes()` fits every combination of family, between-variance
restriction and number of group classes in one call. The `model` column names
each candidate for `get_candidate()`.

```{r enumerate}
grid <- enumerate_classes(ratings, c("climate", "support"), "team",
                          family = c("additive", "dispersion",
                                     "additive_dispersion"),
                          n_group_classes = 1:3, seed = 1)
get_results(grid, "best")
```

The lowest BIC belongs to two additive classes with equal between-group
spread, the model chosen above. Adding class-specific within-group variances
(additive-dispersion) does not improve the fit enough to pay for them, and the
dispersion family, whose classes differ only in spread, fits much worse: these
teams differ in level, not in how much their members disagree.

```{r plot-enumerate, eval = has_ggplot}
plot(grid)
```

Whether two classes are needed at all is a test of one class against two. The
likelihood-ratio statistic has no chi-square reference distribution there, so
`bootstrap_lrt()` simulates it from the one-class fit:

```{r bootstrap}
one_class <- get_candidate(grid, n_group_classes = 1, model = "additive_equal")
two_classes <- get_candidate(grid, n_group_classes = 2, model = "additive_equal")
bootstrap_lrt(one_class, two_classes, iter = 19, n_starts = 3, seed = 1)
```

With 19 replicates the smallest attainable p-value is 0.05; a report uses
several hundred replicates.

## Parameters

Every parameter, with Wald standard errors from the observed information:

```{r parameters}
get_results(fit)
```

The warning comes from a check on each class's *effective groups*: the
number of groups the class would hold in a perfectly classified sample that
pins down the class weight as precisely as this fit does. It is shown in the `group_classes` table below.
Here the strained class has about 38 effective groups of the 49 it is expected
to hold, so most of the information survives the classification; the class is
simply not large. With fewer than 50 effective groups, the simulation study described under *Known limitations* found interval coverage for class parameters starting to fall below 95%, and
far below it when a class is also poorly separated.

`level` separates the three kinds of parameter: `"between"` rows are the
class means and between-group variances, `"within"` rows the within-group
variances shared by the classes (`group_class = "shared"`), and
`"group_class"` rows the class weights. Intervals for variances are formed on
the log scale and for weights on the logit scale, so they stay in range.
Cluster-robust (sandwich) standard errors over teams take one argument:

```{r robust}
get_results(fit, "parameters", vcov_type = "robust")
```

## Groups and their intercepts

Each team's class probabilities, and its modal class:

```{r groups}
head(get_results(fit, "groups"))
get_results(fit, "group_classes")
```

The posterior mean of each team's intercept shrinks its observed average
towards its class mean, more so for small teams; its variance includes the
uncertainty about which class the team belongs to.

```{r intercepts}
head(get_results(fit, "intercepts"))
```

Because the teams were simulated, the classification can be checked against
the true type:

```{r recovery}
get_results(fit, "recovery", data = ratings, truth = "type")
```

Every supportive team is in one class; most strained teams are in the other,
and the few placed with the supportive teams are those whose ratings happened
to fall close to that class.

```{r check, include = FALSE}
# Guards on the prose above: it must stay true of the rendered numbers.
bic_classes <- BIC(fit_one, fit, fit_three)
stopifnot(
  which.min(bic_classes$BIC) == 2L,
  BIC(fit_equal) < BIC(fit), AIC(fit_equal) < AIC(fit),
  any(fit_three$between_zero)
)
classes <- get_results(fit, "group_classes")
stopifnot(min(classes$effective_groups) < 50,
          min(classes$effective_groups) > 30,
          min(classes$effective_groups / classes$count) > 0.7)
recovery <- get_results(fit, "recovery", data = ratings, truth = "type")
agreement <- with(recovery, sum(tapply(n, assigned, max)) / sum(n))
stopifnot(agreement >= 0.9,
          with(subset(recovery, truth == "supportive"), max(share) > 0.9))
```

## Plots

```{r plot-means, eval = has_ggplot}
plot(fit)
```

```{r plot-variances, eval = has_ggplot}
plot(fit, what = "variances")
```

```{r plot-intercepts, eval = has_ggplot}
plot(fit, what = "intercepts")
```

## Cross-level families

When the same ratings define both individual profiles and group classes, the
cross-level families follow the manifest specification of Houle et al.
(2026): each group's means of the indicators are the group-level indicators
of its class. In the *full* family, the group classes also differ in how
their members are distributed over the individual profiles; in the
*restricted* family they do not, and the two levels are estimated separately.
Here, the course enrolments of `course_engagement` form engagement profiles and students
form group classes.

```{r cross-level}
activity <- c("browse", "lectures", "forum_read", "forum_post", "attendance")
full <- multilpa(course_engagement, activity, "student", n_profiles = 2,
                 n_group_classes = 2, family = "full_cross_level", seed = 1)
restricted <- multilpa(course_engagement, activity, "student", n_profiles = 2,
                       n_group_classes = 2, family = "restricted_cross_level",
                       seed = 1)
get_results(full, "composition")
rbind(get_results(full, "fit"), get_results(restricted, "fit"))
```

In the full model one class of students has most of its enrolments in one
profile and the other class mostly in the other. The fits warn that their
criteria cannot show this is real. A group mean is computed from the same
ratings, so these likelihoods count the data twice: on simulated data in which
group membership has no effect, the BIC of the full form preferred two group classes in all 18 simulated data
sets examined. The `fit` table therefore does not choose the number of
group classes or the form, and it is not comparable with the group-class
families above. Standard errors are not reported. Evidence for the classes has
to come from outside these criteria, such as an ordinary `family = "profiles"`
fit to the same data, whose BIC did not prefer group classes in those data sets.

```{r plot-composition, eval = has_ggplot}
plot(full, what = "composition")
```

```{r check-families, include = FALSE}
best <- get_results(grid, "best")
dispersion_two <- subset(get_results(grid),
                         n_group_classes == 2 & model == "dispersion")
additive_two <- subset(get_results(grid),
                       n_group_classes == 2 & model == "additive_equal")
full_fit <- get_results(full, "fit")
restricted_fit <- get_results(restricted, "fit")
composition <- get_results(full, "composition")
stopifnot(best$model == "additive_equal", best$n_group_classes == 2,
          dispersion_two$bic > additive_two$bic + 50,
          full_fit$log_likelihood > restricted_fit$log_likelihood + 100,
          full_fit$bic < restricted_fit$bic,
          full_fit$n_parameters == restricted_fit$n_parameters + 1,
          max(composition$share) > 0.75)
```

## When the between-group variance is zero

In `course_engagement` the student types are discrete by construction, so
students of the same class do not differ in their average activity: the
between-group variance is zero. The fit says so, and the tables report no
standard errors, because a variance on the edge of its space breaks the
approximation Wald inference relies on.

```{r boundary}
activity <- c("browse", "lectures", "forum_read", "forum_post", "attendance")
fit_boundary <- multilpa(course_engagement, activity, "student",
                         n_group_classes = 3, family = "additive",
                         between_variance = "equal", seed = 1)
get_results(fit_boundary, "fit")
```

## Known limitations

A predeclared simulation study (1000 datasets per condition; the report is in
the package repository under `validation/ADDITIVE_SIMULATION.md`) found:

* With a few hundred groups and well-separated classes, means, weights and
  variances are recovered and 95% intervals cover close to 95%.
* Between-group variances are estimated slightly low, the usual small-sample
  bias of maximum likelihood for a variance component; it shrinks as the
  number of groups grows.
* With heavy-tailed ratings, the observed-information standard errors of the
  within-group variances are too small; `vcov_type = "robust"` corrects them.
  With few groups (about 50), prefer the observed-information standard errors.
* When one class is small and poorly separated from another, intervals can
  be badly miscalibrated. The `latents_weak_class` warning (fewer than 50
  effective groups in a class) flagged every such simulated dataset and under
  1% of the well-separated ones with about 100 groups per class; it also
  flags designs with fewer than about 50 groups per class, where coverage
  was mildly low.
* When a between-group variance may truly be zero, its Wald interval is not
  meaningful: either the fit is on the boundary and standard errors are
  withheld, or the interval excludes zero by construction.
